n: Offering a sick or defective animal treated God with contempt. Sacrifices must be whole and the best one has.
Moses describes a case of covenant-breaking by an individual Israelite, man or woman, in any town.

f.g: Breaking the binding agreement made at Sinai.

n: The crime: worshiping other gods, including the sun, moon, and stars, which many ancient peoples revered as deities.
As in chapter 13, a report must be carefully investigated and proven before action is taken.
Once proven, the guilty person was taken outside the town gate and executed by stoning under the law of Moses.

f.g: Outside the city gate, the public place of judgment.

n: A crucial safeguard: no one could be executed on the word of a single witness. At least two or three were required.

f.w: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses

n: Witnesses had to cast the first stones, making them fully responsible for their testimony — a strong check against false accusations.

f.w: The hands of the witnesses shall be first upon him

n: Hard legal cases — about killing, lawsuits, or injuries — that local courts couldn’t resolve were taken to the central sanctuary.
There the Levitical priests and the chief judge would hear the matter and give a ruling, a sort of supreme court.

f.g: Deuteronomy’s usual phrase for the priests from the tribe of Levi.

n: Their verdict was binding. The people must follow it carefully.

f.g: According to the verdict or ruling.

n: Not swerving right or left — a common Deuteronomy image for complete obedience on a straight path.

f.w: to the right hand, nor to the left

n: Defying the high court arrogantly was a capital crime, because it undermined the whole system of justice under God.
The public would take warning and respect lawful authority.
Moses foresees that Israel will one day want a king “like all the nations” — the exact phrase used centuries later in Samuel’s day.

f.w: like as all the nations that are about me

n: Any king must be chosen by God and be a fellow Israelite, not a foreigner.

f.w: whom the LORD thy God shall choose

n: The king must not build up a big chariot force or send people back to Egypt to buy horses. Military might was not to replace trust in God.
No large harem and no hoarding wealth. Solomon broke all three of these limits, and foreign wives turned his heart away — just as warned.
The king had to write his own copy of the law by hand from the priests’ copy. The Greek name “Deuteronomy” comes from the phrase “a copy of this law.”

f.g: Greek Septuagint deuteronomion, “second law” — the source of the book’s name.

n: He was to keep it with him and read it his whole life so he would revere God and obey.

f.w: he shall read therein all the days of his life

n: The law would keep the king humble — no better than his brothers — and secure his dynasty. Even rulers stand under God’s law.

f.w: That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren
